articles.title: Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit
articles.author: Oren Etzioni
paras: In less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley said that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals issue ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

Each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal update at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

On Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”

Last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says his company’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he said at the New York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a company’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.
It will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t update for the next five to 10 years.

Meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute . Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

There’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing , a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign : more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

articles.title: Pikes/Pines | Micro-dramas and bright tail feathers — Capitol Hill’s Dark-eyed Juncos
articles.author: Brendan McGarry
paras: A male Dark-eyed Junco in my parent’s backyard in Seattle. (Image: Brendan McGarry)
As November settles over Capitol Hill and 4:27 PM darkness becomes the daily norm, the neighborhood’s green spaces and parking strips suddenly come alive with low-to-the-ground micro-dramas.

Watching birds in my backyard was my gateway to becoming a birder — they visited our bird feeders, they found food and shelter in my mother’s large garden, they were always doing something interesting if I took the time to pay attention. By far the most ubiquitous species were Dark-eyed Juncos, Junco hyemalis , that showed up in large flocks when fall weather took hold on the Pacific Northwest. Until I became a bit more fluent in the world of birds and our local ecologies, I assumed that they all left for the summer because I didn’t see them for months, until one day I was walking the dog and found a pair of them tirelessly feeding three twittering fledglings in a de facto greenspace adjacent to a local high school. As a fledgling birder, I suddenly realized that things are often more nuanced than flat statements I read in books, and that even common birds have interesting stories to tell.

Dark-eyed Juncos are prettily adorned, small sparrows with dark caps, brown bodies, and eye-catching white outer-tail feathers (this plumage varies a lot by region, but more on that later). But overall they are largely unassuming sparrows that fade into their environment, partially because they also happen to be one of the most abundant birds in North America. Depending on who you ask, their population ranges from 220 million to 630 million. That’s a big variation, but the point is that there are hundreds of millions of juncos across the continent at any one time.
eBird hotspots for Dark-eyed Juncos across the Hill and central Seattle. They are definitely around.

The Hill also has plenty, and you can find juncos just about anywhere with a little bit of greenery, even our most urban blocks. Across the country, and indeed our state, they range from sea level up to the sub-alpine (where they visit to breed and return to moderate climates in winter). Juncos are just about everywhere except extreme deserts, open tundra, and the densest of forests. This ability to roll with a variety of habitats is in part why they remain so abundant despite widespread ecological changes in our world.

Juncos are also birds of the edge lands. They spend their time on the ground or in low shrubs, rarely moving to the tops of trees, except when males fly up high to sing during the breeding season. Food is primarily seeds and other vegetable matter, which they are happy to glean directly from plants, or pick off the ground. Each fall I excitedly wait for the junco flock to return to our yard, flitting in to bend over all the old flower heads of native plants I’ve left to seed. Juncos are around in the summer too, but paired up, on territory, and feeding their young endless invertebrates, shifting their diet to closer to 50/50 plant and vegetable matter.

This shift of food preferences and their breeding behavior are part of the reason I never saw juncos during the summers at my childhood home in North Seattle. Juncos typically nest on or very near the ground, and young leave the nest before they can actually fly because sitting and waiting till they can leaves them vulnerable. We had a dog and an outdoor cat, so despite my mom’s landscaping being quite inviting to juncos, it wasn’t a good place to nest nor for flightless young to roam. Our bird feeders were likewise less attractive to juncos and other birds who focus on the bonanza of insects during warmer months. Besides, the nearby greenspace likely offered more invertebrates because many of our neighbors used insecticides on their landscaping, which are often undiscerning in what insects they target and effectively remove major food sources.
A young Dark-eyed Junco that probably just learned to fly. (Image: Brendan McGarry)

Dark-eyed Juncos may be a common bird, but this abundance and their relatively obliging behavior has made them the star of many studies about North American songbirds. Juncos helped us gain a greater understanding of annual hormonal cycles in birds, offered up good opportunities to study avian dominance and hierarchy structures within flocks, and are even among the species that helped debunk the idea that birds can’t smell. Researchers have demonstrated that juncos can tell each other apart by the scent of the oils they produce in the uropygial gland at the base of their tail. Most birds use oils from this gland when preening, helping waterproof their plumage and likely protecting them from microbial wear. In the case of juncos this also helps them smell each other apart, and even pick a successful, good smelling mate.

We are lucky to have these plucky little birds year-round on the Hill, and their numbers swell right about now, when the juncos who went to breed at higher elevations return to saner wintering grounds. But despite being widespread in North America, some juncos only show up to winter across a large swath of the lower 48 and don’t breed there at all. A lot of people still call them by their old name, Snowbird. And, the birds we call juncos, and those people across the midwest and eastern US might call snowbirds, don’t look entirely identical.
A “Slate-colored Junco,” the bird a lot of people call snowbirds. (Image: USFWS)

Many widespread bird species have sub-populations with very different plumages, body sizes, and even behaviors. Just like Red-tailed Hawks and Song Sparrows – Dark-eyed Juncos have strong geographic variation, particularly noticeable in their coloration. We have “Oregon” Juncos on the Hill and across the Pacific States, while the classic snowbirds of back east are called Slate-colored Juncos (in this situation I guess Oregon means more brown). The variety of junco plumages flummoxed early taxonomists and at one point ornithologists considered today’s Dark-eyed Juncos to be five different species until genetic work demonstrated low variation between populations. Across their range juncos are still mostly doing junco things – spending time on the ground, with similar vocalizations, and eating a lot of seeds.

Despite these similarities and ornithologists’ choice to call Dark-eyed Juncos a single species, recent research suggests that we are witnessing the beginning of a rapid speciation within the genus Junco . Dark-eyed Juncos appear to have expanded into North America after the last ice age, likely speciating from a related species that lives in the mountains of Southern Arizona, New Mexico, and Mexico, the Yellow-eyed Junco, Junco phaeonotus . Under this context, the difference in color, migration patterns, body size, and overall behavior that we see in different Dark-eyed Junco populations across North America is quite exciting (at least to ornithologists, evolutionary biologists, and me), and has happened quite fast – most vertebrates don’t speciate over the course of ten thousand years.
A fun image of extant Junco species and Dark-eyed Junco subspecies, across North and Central America from the Lab of Borja Milá at Museo Nacional de Ciencias Naturales in Madrid, Spain .

Though I appreciate all the various things Dark-eyed Juncos might represent to science, I don’t necessarily need all that to appreciate them. I love when I get a calm moment and can sit still and watch them work through the yard – I witness micro-dramas over food, hear their near constant vocalizations from muttered twitters to emphatic clicks, and when something scares up the flock, the garden is awash in flashes of their white outer tail feathers. Every winter I also wait for that first trilling song, because Dark-eyed Juncos are one of the first birds to begin singing in earnest as the days lengthen. Even now, as I find myself in near darkness at 5pm, I am warmed by the idea of a junco soon to be singing from the top of a tree.

articles.title: Best Side Cycling Tests Out New Henderson Bike Lane in Rainier Beach
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Hanoch of the Youtube channel Best Side Cycling visited an important new protected bike facility in Southeast Seattle, which upgraded safety conditions on the crash-prone corridor of S Henderson Street. The new facility safely connects Be'er Sheva Park and Rainier Beach School in the east to the Chief Sealth Trail farther west, linking destinations like South Shore K-8 school and Rainier Beach Pool and Community Center along the way.

The Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) incorporated Toronto-style concrete barriers on much of the facility to make sure the bike lane is truly protected. Road medians and speed cushions also provide traffic calming on the speeding-prone thoroughfare, aiding all people using the street. With trees still in their fall glory, it's a great time to ride the facility. That said, Hanoch gave the sage advice to tread carefully over piles of leaves as they can be very slippery, especially when wet.

South Seattle has generally trailed North Seattle and the downtown core in getting high-quality protected bike lanes, and that has contributed to it seeing far more fatal crashes and serious traffic injuries than other districts of the city. SDOT reported 71 crashes in the Henderson segment alone from 2021 to 2022, as Best Side Cycling noted, underscoring the need for the project.

However, bit by bit , SDOT is pushing to make up the gap, with the safe streets community long pressing for a more equitable distribution of safe facilities across the city – flagging that South Seattle was getting left behind. Though delayed, major bike network upgrades are planned in South Beacon Hill (extending the recently completed North Beacon Hill bike lane ) and Georgetown .

As for the new Henderson facility, Hanoch's review was positive: "I don't mean to just glaze SDOT, but this one I really do feel they're taking a lot of the best practices they've seen in a lot of different places, and we will use them here, like this daylighting in front of those that parking. It's much bigger than some other places like on Union Street."

articles.title: The life, death and improbable rebirth of LA’s most beloved diner
articles.author: Andrew Gumbel in Los Angeles
paras: For decades, it served pancakes, hash browns and steaks to hungry Angelenos. Then came closure, and a city mourned – but now the Original Pantry is back

Sometimes, an old-school American diner is just a diner. And sometimes, like the Original Pantry in downtown Los Angeles, it feels like the heart and soul of a city, a bellwether of good times and bad.

For decades it was famous for never closing. Located in a low-slung shotgun building on a busy corner, it fed politicians, movie stars, students, criminals and street bums around the clock, seven days a week. The doors had no locks, because the place had no need for them. The portions were huge, the prices dirt cheap, and many of the servers, in bow ties and white shirts, looked like extras from a Harold Lloyd two-reeler.

articles.title: I covered myself in sleep trackers to find the very best
articles.author: Christine Persaud
paras: Get a better night’s sleep with monitoring and guidance from smartwatches, smart rings, smart bands and sleep earbuds
The best sleep masks and best Bluetooth sleep masks

Getting quality sleep is just as crucial as getting enough sleep. And how you feel in the morning only tells part of the story. Smartwatches, smart bands, smart rings and sleep earbuds can all help fill in the details: how long it took you to doze off, how long you spent in deep sleep, how restless you were, your resting heart rate, even if you have night-time breathing difficulties.

Armed with this information, you can learn how your lifestyle affects your sleep. Maybe your after dinner cappuccino triggers a night of tossing and turning, or you’re more restful after evening workouts. As the wise GI Joe once said, knowing is half the battle. And the more you know about your sleep, the better chance you have of improving it.

articles.title: How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?
articles.author: Huw Green
paras: Emotions play a significant part in physical symptoms – but not in the way people often imagine

When Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it?

Some illnesses aren’t caused by disease or damage, but arise when the coordinated functioning of the body goes awry. In a percentage of these cases a person’s psychological health is an important element in their symptoms. Intuitively this seems mysterious. We are accustomed to thinking about physical symptoms as being caused by physical events; viruses, inflammation, bleeding. How can something as intangible as a thought have any impact on something as physical as a leg? How can the mind make us ill?

articles.title: Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.
One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report , released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Testing that more closely replicates the company’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company says it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.
Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend , the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software update that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.
So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July update was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.
That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.
Third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.
The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.
“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report says.

The preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.
The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also plans to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.
Some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft says its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft said the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”

The new testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the company says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

articles.title: Sound Transit Funds Study to Speed Up D Line Bus
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: On Thursday, the Sound Transit Board allocated $500,000 to fund a study of bus speed and reliability improvements for the RapidRide D Line, which runs from Downtown Seattle to Ballard and Crown Hill. It's an early signal that D Line riders can expect a faster ride – a few years down the road, anyway.

King County Executive Girmay Zahilay brought forward the budget amendment, with support from Tukwila Mayor Thomas McLeod and the entire Seattle delegation on the agency board: Mayor Katie Wilson, City Councilmember Dan Strauss, and County Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda.

A timeline for the project was not immediately clear, but supporters noted it was important to provide interim improvements while Ballard and Interbay wait on its delayed light rail project. In 2016, the campaign for the successful Sound Transit 3 (ST3) ballot measure pledged to deliver Ballard Link by 2035, but the timeline has slipped since then.

“I’m very, very happy to be sponsoring this amendment, bringing half a million dollars forward, so that Sound Transit and the City and King County can together work to advance the planning and improve the RapidRide D to Ballard," Wilson said. "We know that that’s no substitute for light rail, but right now it is the third busiest route in King County. It carries more than 10,000 riders a day, and making this bus work better will ease the mobility burden in this regional growth center and keep people moving while we do that longer term work.”

Zahilay credited the Save Ballard Rail coalition with raising the need for D Line improvements. Designing the project will entail a collaboration between Sound Transit, the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT), and King County Metro. While Metro operates the bus, SDOT maintains the roadway over which it runs, and the Seattle Transit Measure also funds extra service that boosts bus frequency.

"I want to specifically thank Save Ballard Rail, who has been regularly in touch with my staff and asked us to look into ways to expedite improvements to the RapidRide D line," Zahilay said. "This amendment would move $500,000 of already committed funding for this project up to 2027 to ensure that Sound Transit, SDOT, and Metro explore options and start planning for these capital improvements that would be intended to speed up the RapidRide D."

Zahilay reminded the board that ST3 included funding for Seattle bus improvements as an early deliverable . Namely, it included $35 million to "design and implement transit priority improvements along King County Metro’s RapidRide C and D lines that provide service to Ballard and West Seattle as an early deliverable to provide improved speed and reliability, in advance of light rail starting operations to these areas."

"When voters approved Sound Transit 3, they approved a modest amount of funding to advance the RapidRide D resources for capital improvements, bus and traffic signal priority, just to help move people in the interim while the light rail station and light rail was getting to Ballard," Zahilay said.

That funding was a victim of the 2021 realignment vote , which delayed a number of projects due to pandemic-related planning delays and budgetary strain. The early deliverable went from an early deliverable to a late deliverable without a definite timeline.

"This was originally designed to be an early deliverable in 2025, but in 2021, the board voted to delay the timeline as part of a realignment plan, and I want to speed things back up again," Zahilay said. "I think this board has made it clear that getting to Market Street in the long term, as the CEO mentioned, is a priority for this board. And we have also said that, in the short term, we want to improve transit service in that area through transit mitigation efforts."

As it stands, Sound Transit's best-case scenario for light rail to reach Ballard is 2042 – although the agency has granted that many hurdles remain and has not ruled out the opening date slipping to the 2060s if those hurdles are not navigated.
Jonatan Gonzalez, an organizer with Save Ballard Rail, spoke in favor of the amendment at Thursday's board meeting.
"As we know, Ballard is waiting for light rail, and we can improve bus service now," Gonzalez said. "That'd be amazing."
Metro spokesperson Jeff Switzer told The Urbanist that Metro, in partnership with SDOT and Sound Transit, had some earlier planning to build upon, but that those concepts would need updating.

"Following voter approval of this investment in 2016, work began to identify projects that would improve speed and reliability along the corridor," Switzer said. "That effort was paused following the initial realignment process, and Metro plans to update the analysis to identify RapidRide D enhancements that can be delivered in the near term for the benefit of riders."

Wilson and Zahilay both emphasized bus improvements in their successful runs in 2025. Zahilay reiterated that accelerating the R Line project , replacing Route 7 in the Rainier Valley, was a priority for his administration, and recently cleared a King County Council committee approval vote .

One of Wilson's signature moves in her first year, meanwhile, was rapidly rolling out a bus lane for Route 8. Long notorious for its lateness, Route 8 has since seen a dramatic jump in speed and reliability thanks to the street redesign, a project her predecessor, Bruce Harrell, had sought to frame as completely infeasible.

The same style treatment for the D Line could result in huge time savings for riders. The route lacks consistent bus lanes outside of downtown, with SDOT offering brief sections a few blocks at a time rather than a connected treatment.

Another big move for Wilson was a renewal proposal that doubled the size of the Seattle Transit Measure, which will provide funding to boost frequencies on about a dozen bus lines , with the D a likely candidate. The transit measure passed resoundingly in November with more than 72% of the vote.

With the D Line study just now getting off the ground, the scope of the project is not yet clear. Strauss floated the idea of an express bus with reduced stops shadowing the route. He also underscored how slow the bus is now.

"I will state: that RapidRide is very slow," Strauss said. "It is a milk-run bus out to Ballard going through Uptown. Its travel times are 40 to 45 minutes from where you sit right now just to downtown Ballard."
As riders reacted to the news, some disputed the trip times Strauss has quoted as exagerrated.

"Why does he feel the need to pad everything? It's 27 to 36 minutes from Pioneer Square to Market Street depending on time of day," Seattle Transit Blog contributor David Lawson wrote in a Bluesky post . "Lots of room for improvement, but the work that's already been done has made a difference."

One joked that Strauss did not know what a milk run is, alluding to the D's straight rather than circuitous routing. On the other hand, another D Line rider noted reliability and bus bunching issues can add wait times at stops.

Strauss has mentioned on multiple occasions that he thinks the routing through Uptown to serve Seattle Center slows the route down too much. The drawback would be that skipping the Seattle Center would decrease Northwest Seattle's access to that popular destination, and it may require shifting another route over to provide adequate coverage for Uptown.
One way or the other, improvements appear inbound, although just how dramatic and imminent is yet to be determined.

"The RapidRide D Line serves 10,500 riders on an average weekday and is the third busiest route in the region. It provides critical connections between Ballard, Interbay, Uptown, and Downtown Seattle, while also linking customers to other frequent transit services throughout the city," Switzer said. "We look forward to partnering with Sound Transit and SDOT to advance improvements that enhance reliability, speed, and the overall customer experience on this important corridor."

articles.title: Army’s plan to blow up aging explosives will spread lead over part of Iowa – what you need to know about the risks
articles.author:
<name>Patrick O'Shaughnessy, Professor of Occupational and Environmental Health, University of Iowa</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/patrick-oshaughnessy-2779785"/>
paras: The U.S. Army set off waves of anxiety in Iowa when it confirmed plans to carry out two controlled explosions at an ammunition facility there with just a few days’ notice . According to the Army, dozens of old barrels containing lead azide , an explosive used as a detonator, have become unstable and pose an “ unacceptable risk of accidental detonation .” Intentionally detonating the barrels is considered the best option for controlling the risk, the Army determined.

However, the explosions are expected to release a large plume of lead particles, and lead is a neurotoxin. The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is in Middletown, a town of about 360 residents in southeast Iowa. People and farms would be in the path of the plume as the wind blows it for miles.

The detonations were briefly delayed after the backlash and rescheduled for Nov. 23, 2026 . A federal appeals court separately paused the Army’s emergency Environmental Protection Agency permit for the detonations after two groups sued, but the U.S. Justice Department argued that the permit wasn’t necessary in the face of an immediate threat.
The Justice Department told the court in a response late on Nov. 21 that the Army intends to carry out the detonations by Nov. 24, 2026 . A precise date and time weren’t immediately released.

To better understand the risks, we asked Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa, what people in the region would face. O'Shaughnessy is part of a team scrambling to have testing in place when the Army carries out its detonation plan.

If you picture a dust plume, it carries particulate matter that can get into the lungs as you breathe. In this case, we’re talking about small particles that contain lead, which is toxic to humans and pets .

Those particles will settle over the area downwind of the detonation site. First it’s air pollution – if you’re outside, you can inhale those particles. Then it becomes surface pollution. The lead dust can get on your hands and into your body. The big concern there is for young children . If you think about 2-year-olds, they put everything in their mouths.

Lead is easily absorbed by the body. It gets into the bloodstream, and it can cause harm to just about every major organ in our bodies , including the nervous system and the brain. It tends to hide out in bones and teeth , where it can leach out and cause harm.

Studies have shown lead exposure is a major concern for pregnant women with developing fetuses. In young children, lead exposure can slow their brain development. Long-standing results from studies have demonstrated a reduction in IQ in children with chronic lead exposure, such as from lead-based paint in old houses.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says there is no safe level of lead in the body . That’s a pretty strong statement.
Where this plume travels and how far depends primarily on the wind speed and direction in the hours after the explosions.

We have a sense of what happens from studying pollution from smokestacks. Smokestacks are tall for a reason – they eject the pollutants high into the atmosphere so the pollutants dilute as they drift downwind.

In this case, instead of a steady stream coming out of the smokestack, it’s going to be a big puff that will literally create a cloud. That cloud will rise and start dissipating as it is diluted in the air. It will become invisible at some point, but that doesn’t mean the lead isn’t there.

If the Army had blown up those storage containers on Nov. 20, as initially planned, the forecast was for a fairly strong 15-mile-per-hour surface wind. The plume would have mostly diluted by the time it reached I-80, which is where I’m sitting, about 80 miles to the north.

If the Army goes through with its rescheduled plan on Nov. 23 , the preliminary forecast is for much slower wind blowing toward the south-southeast. Slower wind means the plume would affect a smaller area, but people there would experience a higher concentration of lead as it slowly floats by.
That may mean fewer people are affected, but the exposure could be more intense. We won’t know exactly what people will experience until it happens.
Honestly, I would find a way to get out of the area for the day. If you can’t leave, the Army has a list of precautions that people should take, and I think those are good recommendations.

The Army is advising people near the plant to vacate their homes during the detonation and others to shelter in place. That means staying indoors and closing all your doors and windows. If you can, shut off the furnace – it pulls in air that could be contaminated as the plume travels through an area.
Within a few hours, the plume will have dissipated or moved on. But that doesn’t mean the lead disappears. It falls to the ground, meaning you and your pets can still get it on you.

After the plumed dissipates, the Army suggests getting a hose and spraying down window sills, cars, any horizontal surfaces where the dust can accumulate. Car door handles can easily collect and transfer the lead to people. If you have children’s play areas or toys outside, wash those down.

Lead is a persistent compound – there’s no way to degrade it. Washing it off surfaces transfers the lead to the soil. At this point in the year, the majority of the crops have been harvested, so there’s less risk of lead settling on plants in farm fields. However, some dairy farmers are concerned about their cows getting into lead that settles on grass.
Our results from sampling during and after the plume should help people better understand the risks.

My colleagues and I will be looking at two aspects of potential exposure to lead: the airborne dust, which we’ll collect with instruments during the plume to get the lead concentration, and then dust that settles on surfaces and the ground, which we’ll collect with gauzelike pads and send to a lab for analysis.
The lab will be able to tell how much lead is in those samples, and the air samples will let us calculate how much people were exposed to the lead.

This is all happening last minute – we only found out about the plan a few days before the Army initially planned to detonate the barrels. Thankfully, the university and our federal- and state-funded centers have the people and technology to quickly carry out testing. We hope to have results about a week after it happens. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also has a team that will be doing sampling.
This article, originally published Nov. 21, 2026, has been updated with a Justice Department statement that the Army plans to act by Nov. 24. The date and time were not immediately specified.
Patrick O'Shaughnessy receives funding from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences

articles.title: Microsoft ‘To Do’ users make a big to-do over popular task app’s pending retirement
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal users that Microsoft To Do would be their new home. Now it’s asking them to switch again.

Microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the company’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.
The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X : “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”

That’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

The catch for personal users: Microsoft’s support page says the To Do apps are also retiring for personal Microsoft accounts, including paid Microsoft 365 Personal and Family subscribers, and that Planner isn’t available for those accounts. Microsoft hasn’t announced a replacement for them.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft says Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps : no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.
He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Why Microsoft is doing it: The company said putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A new Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.
The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”

Users weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.
“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.
Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday users, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft announced Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

Rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist , which called itself “the natural successor” and said it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

Reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent company, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.
Now some of those former Wunderlist users may end up back with the people who built it.

articles.title: Startup Spotlight: An engineer’s search for better, safer baby products led him to launch Birch
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: A new baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.
But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.
“We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla said. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

To spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch , an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.
The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

Birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has issues with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and New Jersey.
Gangiredla said the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.
If you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla said. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”

The platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for users.
We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.
In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch

Birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.
What problem are you obsessed with solving?

The impossible research burden on new parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.
What surprised you after talking to customers?

How universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — big metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.
How has AI changed the way you build your company?

It’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.
What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

That “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.
What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.
What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.
…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Sound Transit Bingo
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: To celebrate 30 years since voters passed Sound Move , Sound Transit is hosting a transit Bingo game today. Sound Move was the Central Puget Sound Regional Transit Authority’s first voter approved funding package to build a regional transit system. The Sound Transit brand was not adopted until 1997. Sound Move included commuter rail between Everett-Seattle and Lakewood-Seattle, light rail in Tacoma and between Seattle-SeaTac, and an extensive network of express buses in Snohomish, King, and Pierce counties.

The first component of Sound Move to enter service, ST Express, began on September 19, 1999 with nine routes. Commuter rail service started the following year with trips between Seattle and Tacoma. The agency’s first light rail line, then-called Tacoma Link, opened in August 2003. Light rail service in Seattle, Central Link, began service on July 18, 2009 between downtown Seattle and Tukwila.

Everyone is invited to explore the region while visiting stations to fill in their Bingo card today between 10am to 2pm. The first 450 people to complete a row, column, or diagonal and return their card to a designated drop-off will get a 30th Anniversary ORCA card . Everyone who gets Bingo will be entered into a raffle to win additional prizes. If you want to go above and beyond, complete every square for a chance to win a grand prize that includes one year of free transit and a behind-the-scenes ride-along through a Link train wash. articles.title: Thanks to new generation of office space, Capitol Hill’s daytime population ranges from Duolingo to start-ups
articles.author: CHS
paras: CENTRL Office’s Capitol Hill Location (Image: Matt Freire)
Building out a traditional office on Capitol Hill comes with real overhead — even for small upgrades.

According to City of Seattle construction permits signed off this month, language-learning giant Duolingo spent a base $18,000 on interior alterations just to add a dedicated lactation room inside its fifth-floor offices inside the net-zero energy Bullitt Center at 15th and Madison

While established companies can absorb bespoke buildouts and permitting timelines, Capitol Hill’s smaller office rentals and coworking spaces are giving homegrown entrepreneurs an affordable alternative, offering shared amenities and flexible footprints without the upfront capital expense.

As remote and hybrid work spaces reshape how businesses utilize office space, coworking and office rentals are seeing an increased interest from freelancers and small teams, according to the developers behind the spaces.

While overall Seattle office vacancy remained elevated at 27.7% in Q3 2026, it has begun edging down from its peak and neighborhood submarkets are faring substantially better than the downtown core, according to commercial real estate firm Kidder Mathews . In the Capitol Hill and Central District submarket, total vacancy stood at 10.5% across 4.8 million square feet of inventory, compared to 35% downtown. Locally, Capitol Hill’s CENTRL Office reported a 30% increase in occupancy over the past year.
Kaitee Quinn , general manager at CENTRL, said that these environments are becoming an essential stepping stone in business growth today.

“I think we’re filling a need that has been created by everybody preferring remote and hybrid work now,” Quinn said. “You get to choose to come to a space that’s beautiful, that’s lively, and meet people in your neighborhood.”

Duolingo’s own Capitol Hill footprint followed that trajectory. Before signing its direct lease at the Bullitt Center, the company’s Seattle team operated out of coworking desks inside the historic Kelly-Springfield building on 11th Ave — the same space CENTRL Office now operates.

As regulatory and operating costs rise across the city, these smaller office rentals and coworking spaces give entrepreneurial companies the traditional workplace benefits without having to front the operational expenses.

Different from coworking spaces, the Ballou Wright building on 12th Avenue offers separate office leases for businesses looking for a more traditional workplace. Jill Cronauer, president of Hunters Capital, which owns and manages the Ballou Wright building, said that these spaces are becoming the cost-effective option for small teams.

“There’s a huge distinction about small office space that’s super critical because it’s more affordable,” Cronauer said. “It’s also acting as an essential step down if an organization is resizing and downsizing.”

Cronauer also highlighted the importance of Capitol Hill’s creative atmosphere and access to mass transit as attractive features for businesses. The Ballou Wright building houses many independent tenants, such as marketers, interior designers and architecture firms.

Liz Dunn , developer of The Cloud Room and Chophouse Row , said the coworking space has become a launching pad for many independent businesses, some of which she said eventually grow beyond what the space can provide.

“We always have noticed and love the fact that we have been able to incubate little companies that have then gone on to grow,” Dunn said. “Sometimes we are able to incubate a Cloud Room member company into a user of a different office space at Chophouse. It gives us enormous satisfaction to play that role.”

Locally, shared workspaces have served as launchpads for Seattle’s startups and small businesses. On Capitol Hill, food and drink entrepreneur Makini Howell moved her administrative team into The Cloud Room, where she collaborated with fellow tenant and graphic design studio Wildern on the brand’s identity. Meanwhile, spaces like Foundations on Boylston and CENTRL Office on 11th host dozens of early-stage technical founders. Across the city, coworking hubs and incubators including The Pioneer Collective, 9Zero, AI House , and Waterfront Workspaces have helped launch notable local ventures ranging from screen-free kids’ phone maker Tin Can and proptech startup YIMBY AI to applied-AI companies Lexion, Yoodli, and Vercept .

Some of these offices offer amenities like large meeting rooms, private phone booths, Wi-Fi and coffee in their memberships, which cuts a lot of the overhead costs associated with a traditional office building.
For larger employers, taking on traditional commercial leases and custom tenant improvements remains standard practice.

Pittsburgh-based Duolingo, which employs roughly 900 people globally and operates a regional engineering and product outpost of a few dozen staffers in Capitol Hill, signed a lease in 2024 for 7,940 square feet of office space inside the six-story Bullitt Center. Leasing an entire floorplate in one of the neighborhood’s signature commercial buildings gives the publicly traded edtech company room to customize its own workspace — while underscoring the gap between institutional tech tenants and the solo founders or small teams turning to shared spaces to avoid buildout costs.
In addition to providing independent businesses support, Dunn also said that office space plays an important role for the economy and the identity of the neighborhood.
“A truly successful 24/7 neighborhood has to have residents, retail, and office,” Dunn said. “And I wish we had more office space on Capitol Hill than we do.”
