articles.title: Seattle launches community process to rename Jackson Park — Jackson Street? Not yet
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Mayor Katie Wilson has directed Seattle Parks and Recreation to launch a public process to rename north Seattle’s Jackson Park , responding to what she says are community calls for a title that better reflects the land’s history and the city’s values.

Originally named after President Andrew Jackson whose policies forcibly displaced Native American peoples, the park at 1000 NE 135th has faced scrutiny from residents questioning the legacy. The renaming initiative coincides with new light rail service and planned pedestrian and bicycle upgrades designed to improve neighborhood access to the park and its golf course.
“With new light rail connections and opportunities to make the park more accessible and welcoming, we should have a park that reflects the values of our city,” Wilson said.
Groups have also pushed for better community use of the park, including tough questions about the future of the golf course and potential for future affordable housing development.
Under the City’s Park Naming Policy, SPR is inviting residents to submit name proposals by Monday, December 14th.

The parks naming committee will evaluate suggestions based on the land’s history, natural features, geographical location, and cultural significance, including Indigenous ties to the area. Proposals may also honor a community contributor deceased for at least three years. Written submissions, including a brief rationale, can be sent via email to PKS_BPRC@seattle.gov. The committee will review the entries and recommend a final choice to the department superintendent.
The debate over Jackson Park also draws attention to Seattle’s other prominent Andrew Jackson namesake: South Jackson Street.

The major thoroughfare through Pioneer Square, the Chinatown–International District, and the Central District was platted by city co-founder David “Doc” Maynard in 1853. While periodic community proposals have called for renaming the street—or symbolically rededicating it to a different figure without changing addresses , similar to how King County was rededicated from Vice President William Rufus King to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. —any formal street name change requires a Seattle City Council ordinance and involves significant logistical hurdles for affected residents, businesses, and transit agencies.

Jackson is far from the only Seattle landmark with a contested history; Maynard’s original 1853 street grid also honored pro-slavery and secessionist politicians on neighboring South King Street (William Rufus King) and South Lane Street (Joseph Lane), while other city streets and parks commemorate slaveholders like James Madison and Thomas Jefferson, as well as territorial Governor Isaac Stevens, who coerced local Indigenous tribes into ceding their lands.
Alongside the renaming effort, SPR is gathering broader feedback on park safety, cleanliness, and trail conditions through an upcoming online survey.

articles.title: Hollingsworth celebrates $6M economic growth fund for Central District and Southeast Seattle in final budget push
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: As the full Seattle City Council prepares for one last vote finalizing the city’s 2027-2028 budget, District 3 representative and Council President Joy Hollingsworth is celebrating the inclusion of a $6 million economic growth fund she championed to power community investments in the Central District and Southeast Seattle.

Seattle’s Select Budget Committee approved the budget amendment sponsored by Hollingsworth allocating $3.2 million in 2027 and $2.8 million in 2028 to the Central District/Southeast Seattle Fund . According to Hollingsworth, the measure aims to “preserve cultural heritage and foster economic growth” across District 3 and South Seattle.
The program will serve as a “targeted reinvestment mechanism” for community-led initiatives, cultural institutions, and small businesses, Hollingsworth says.

“Supporting community organizations, small businesses and people that preserve and revitalize the Central District and southeast Seattle communities is why this fund exists,” Hollingsworth said, thanking budget chair Dan Strauss and co-sponsors Councilmembers Dionne Foster and Rob Saka .

Beginning in 2027, the Seattle Department of Neighborhoods will manage the funds via a “structured and transparent application process” supported by two full-time staff members. Department director Quynh Pham noted that local organizations play a vital role in preserving the area’s “history, culture, and sense of belonging.”

Friday’s final vote will a contentious week in which council members approved more than 100 amendments to Mayor Katie Wilson’s spending plan, which had originally been shaped to close a projected $175 million shortfall without dipping into reserves or new taxes. Council changes included a decision to raid $31 million in JumpStart payroll tax reserves to cover council amendments to Wilson’s proposal. The tax was originally shaped to fund affordable housing and services coming out of the pandemic.
The full council is expected to pass the 2027-2028 spending plan Friday but Councilmember Maritza Rivera said she will not vote for the budget.

“I cannot in good conscience recommend this budget. It is not fiscally responsible or sustainable,” Rivera said in a statement. “This budget continues the bad habit of adding without balancing and relying, in part, on JumpStart reserves to cover those adds. This undoes our previous commitment to rebuild the JumpStart reserves. It is simply bad budgeting.”
The full City Council will vote on the final 2027-2028 budget Friday at 1 PM before sending it to the mayor for signature.

articles.title: Jackson Street Housing Project Could Leave King County on Hook for Millions
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A proposal from King County Executive Girmay Zahilay to finance an affordable housing project is raising some eyebrows at the County Council, due to a draft lease agreement that could leave the County's general fund on the hook for unexpected cost increases for years down the line. The project, at 701 S Jackson Street in Seattle's Chinatown-International District (CID), would include 111 new, mostly family-sized units along with retail space but also turn King County into a tenant charged with paying off bonds used for building construction.

The ordinance currently in front of the County Council would provide financing to a $63.8 million apartment building that has been stalled for many years. Developers Nitze-Stagen and the Housing Diversity Corporation, operating as a joint entity called O.Z. Navigator, secured permits for 701 S Jackson Street in 2022 as a 238-unit building, mostly one-bedroom units and studios.

Going in on a site previously owned by the CID's storied Mar family, the former gas station required significant site remediation work to make it suitable for housing. And even though that remediation work is now complete, the construction project was never able to move forward due to financing issues.

Six years later, the project has been redesigned with far more family-sized units, making it more attractive to public financers following an oversaturation of Seattle's studio and one-bedroom affordable housing market. Of 111 total apartments, 96 would be two-bedrooms, and 14 would be three-bedroom, all available to residents making 67% of King County's area median income or below – around $90,000 per year for a family of three. Designs include one one-bedroom unit.

Included in a slate of housing investments tucked into Zahilay's proposed mid-biennial budget update this fall, the 701 S Jackson project was notable in that it was missing a specific dollar commitment, in contrast with line items like a $4 million earmark for the Pacific Tower Quarters Building in Beacon Hill and $1.8 million for a veteran's housing project in Kirkland.
That's because the deal in the International District would be structured very differently than the other projects.

Under the ordinance that could be voted on as soon as December 8, King County would serve as the third party on a Development Services Agreement with the Housing Diversity Corporation and a nonprofit specifically set up for the project, 701 Essential Housing. That entity would issue up to $90 million in tax-exempt bonds to build the project, with Housing Diversity Corporation the developer.

"Upon completion of construction, the Master Lease Agreement would be effective, allowing the County to lease the property from 701 Essential Housing," a staff report from late October noted. "On behalf of the County, 701 Essential Housing would manage subleases for residential and retail tenants. The County would make payments to 701 Essential Housing to cover any remaining debt service and operations costs not covered by sublease revenue. At the end of the 30-year lease term and full repayment of the bonds, the County would assume ownership of the property."

In the financial scenario envisioned by Zahilay's office, the County would be responsible for paying $37.5 million over the life of the project, with a maximum annual payment of around $2.5 million in 2032 that ramps down over time.

King County Chief Budget Officer Aaron Rubardt told councilmembers that the County's general fund, under significant strain in recent years by restrictions on property tax growth and limited growth in unincorporated areas outside cities, is currently tabbed as the primary source of revenue for the project. But Rubardt also noted that another funding source could be found at a later time – potentially the countywide housing levy that Zahilay has been formally considering since shortly after taking office.

"The proposal is for the general fund to back this, and we built into our general fund projections that the general fund would pay the debt service," Rubardt told councilmembers. "But over time, the Executive and Council can make a decision to have another funding source fund it. So I think that is fungible over time. So keep that in mind, it doesn't all have to be paid by the general fund, but the obligation that we're signing up for does obligate the general fund as the backer of the debt."

A $37.5 million general fund contribution to fund 111 units would amount to one of the largest set-asides for an individual affordable housing project in King County history. The proposed investment works out to just over $337,000 per unit, albeit spaced out over 30 years.

In 2025, King County’s Housing Finance Program awarded $23.7 million to eight projects total, helping to advance a collective total of 672 homes – however, all of those projects were receiving additional financing on top of any County contribution.

But as laid out in staff analysis presented during Tuesday's work session, the county's contribution isn't fixed in place. Various scenarios could play out that would balloon that number, including lower-than-expected occupancy of the rental units, increased construction costs, and higher interest rates.

With a 30% increase in project costs, the staff presentation noted, the County contribution could end up at $77.2 million, doubling the amount in projected pro-forma plan that the Zahilay administration presented. With a 1% more expensive bond coupon, costs could go up by $20 million. A vacancy rate at 701 S Jackson Street that is double what's currently expected could cost the County an additional $13 million, despite the fact that the County would not be in control of managing the rentals itself.
Even more worrying for the general fund is the fact that these scenarios could all occur to various degrees, with nothing constraining the top cost that the County would be held responsible for.
"It is not possible to predict which of these scenarios, or which combination, might occur," this week's updated staff report noted.

During the meeting, Rubardt faced questions about why the deal was structured in this specific way, with Rubardt pointing to the need to stand up affordable units quickly. A slowdown in development traced to higher interest rates and higher operating costs for existing affordable housing buildings does mean that there are fewer shovel-ready projects that the County could plug itself into.

"The priority was for 111 family-sized units in the International District, two bedrooms and three bedrooms," Rubardt said. "The reason we are proposing this now under this arrangement is that we think it's a fast way, a relatively fast way, to get something built and to open up those affordable housing units, so we can have them open in 2029, hopefully."
Executive's Office spokesperson Callie Craighead provided additional information about Zahilay's decision to turn to this type of lease agreement in a follow-up email to The Urbanist .

"This is a new financing model for the County for funding affordable housing; however, it is not new to the county," Craighead wrote. "King County has used this financing model for other buildings, including office buildings in the downtown office core. This financing model has also been used by local universities to fund dormitories. The County is looking for innovative ways to finance urgent housing needs. "

"This funding arrangement provided the flexibility to fund affordable housing relatively quickly; and at the end of agreement the County will have acquired both the land and facility," Craighead added.

In the rosy scenario, that transfer could provide the County an asset that could operate at a profit, generating a revenue stream for additional public investments in housing or otherwise. In the not-so-rosy scenario, the County could inherit an aging building with a maintenance backlog for which it would continue to be on the hook.

Though Zahilay's office is pushing for a vote on the agreement before the end of 2026, Tuesday's meeting was the first substantive conversation to occur on the proposal at the council level – an October 28 briefing was cancelled due to other agenda items running long.
During the recent work session, several councilmembers raised clear concerns about exposing the general fund to this level of unexpected cost increases.

"I think I heard that it would be difficult for us to legislate to share that risk differently," Councilmember Claudia Balducci said. "Although I would recommend that we try, because you know, if we're taking all of the risk, that's a tough ask for the County's general fund."
Craighead defended Zahilay's approach to managing King County's finances.

"The Executive always scrutinizes allocating limited General Fund dollars and limiting the fiscal risk to the County," Craighead wrote. "As part of his commitment to building a better government, Executive Zahilay’s proposed second omnibus budget maintains the General Fund’s emergency reserves at 8% and the 'rainy day fund.' The Executive and the Budget Team is starting to work through scenario planning for the 2028-2029 budget to minimize risk and deliver a balanced budget."

Following the work session, the council held a closed-door discussion of the legal risks behind the deal, a session held at the request of Councilmember Jorge Barón. If the ordinance is rejected, that would represent the biggest break between Zahilay's office and the County Council so far during his term, with the council largely deferring to Executive branch priorities so far.
On the other hand, it's possible that the council is able to come around to Zahilay's proposal, potentially by putting additional guardrails on the lease agreement.
Balducci noted that if the general fund ends up getting tapped more than expected to meet the County's obligations, that could lead to service cuts elsewhere in County government.
"People lose their jobs, and we end up cutting vital services," Balducci said. "So, I just think we need to be very clear about what risk we're taking on and how good or bad we feel about that."

articles.title: Tacoma Council Axes Crisis Response Team, Slashes City Budget to Address Deficit
articles.author: Carolyn Bick
paras: Facing a major fiscal cliff to the tune of $40 million over the next biennium, the City of Tacoma was forced to make sharp cuts to its 2027-2028 biennial budget, which the Tacoma City Council adopted in a unanimous vote Tuesday.

These cuts included eliminating more than 100 staff positions, 14 of which were filled, as well as cutting the City’s fairly new civilian co-responder Holistic Outreach Promoting Engagement (HOPE) team, and whittling down the police department’s community service officer (CSO) team.

Even though these cost-saving measures reduced the City’s 2027-2028 deficit back down to zero, this doesn’t mean that Tacoma is in the clear for the long term. The City still projects an $18 million budget shortfall by the time the next biennial budget rolls around. By the 2031-2032 biennium, the City will once again face a $40 million shortfall.

Public reaction to the decision to cut the HOPE Team, a program through the Tacoma Fire Department, was especially negative. Several members of the public, including a number of community activists and a representative from the NAACP, called for its retention and for the City to revisit how it dispatched the team. At least one member of the public said that they felt like the city was breaking the promise it had made in the wake of Manuel Ellis’s death in custody of Tacoma police officers in March 2020.

But civilian crisis response is not permanently off the table. The City introduced two amendments that put $150,000 towards a crisis response study and $400,000 toward crisis response and case management support. The latter amendment is meant as a bridge to sustain some capacity for crisis response between HOPE’s elimination and whatever team may replace it. The HOPE team had been budgeted at $4 million over the next two years before the cuts.

The city will also retain five of the 10 total community service officer positions through the Tacoma Police Department. These officers handle non-emergency calls. The City had initially considered entirely eliminating this cohort of officers.
“For years,” a slide in the city’s Oct. 27 budget presentation reads, “the cost of running the City has grown almost twice as fast as the money it collects.”

At that meeting — which served as the first hearing for the proposed biennial budget — the City’s finance director, Andy Cherullo, told councilmembers that the City had been facing a $40 million structural deficit in the General Fund. Without the proposed cuts, he continued, the structural deficit would grow to $75 million by the 2029-2030 biennium, and $106 million by the 2031-2032 biennium.
But this doesn’t mean the City is out of the woods.
“We are still projecting structural deficits in the next couple of biennium,” Cherullo said. “There are further hard decisions in the future for this City Council.”
The impending budget shortfall isn’t for lack of trying — and it isn’t an unfamiliar problem.
State law limits how quickly some revenues can grow. For instance, property tax levies can only grow at a rate of 1% per year.

“There’s no City expense that grows at 1% per year,” Cherullo said. “Just like our community members, the City is not immune to the higher inflation currently in the economy. We are also facing higher costs for fuel, supplies, and services. Benefits like health care are growing at double-digit rates, and there's general uncertainty related to what direction the overall economy will move that can impact other City revenues like sales tax and our business and occupation taxes.”
There is also an increasing demand for City services, and wages, benefits, and supplies cost more every year.
Together, this all creates a difficult situation for the City.

“Unless the state gives us more opportunities to have progressive revenue sources at the local level, we’re going to continue to have these problems year after year after year, and it’s been happening for the last 24 years,” Deputy Mayor Joe Bushnell said at the council’s Nov. 10 meeting. “So people are wondering, ‘Well why can’t the City be creative about these different things?’ It’s because we are struggling to fund basic services as it is. We can’t be as creative as we’d like to be because we don’t have the revenue sources or the options available to us from beyond our powers here.”
In passing the budget, Bushnell was also the only member of the council to acknowledge that the City had cut staffed positions.

“I […] want to recognize that through this budget, we eliminated 100 positions, and behind many of those positions were people, great dedicated staff doing amazing work on behalf of our community,” he said at the Nov. 17 meeting. “A hundred positions have been eliminated out of this budget, and I just don’t want us to lose sight of that fact, because that’s not actually a good thing, I think, for our city, because those are services that are not going to be rendered.”

City Manager Hyun Kim told The Urbanist in a later interview that cutting the 14 filled positions was not an easy decision, and that the City’s Human Resources worked hard to identify where it could keep staff whose positions were originally going to be cut. Prior to budget deliberations, a little more than half of identified positions were filled.

“[W]e got that number down to 14. […] We really did try our best to give as much advance notice to our employees that are impacted employees in those filled positions and that's why we gave the notice, we gave options,” Kim said. “We were not completely successful because as was mentioned last night by our deputy mayor, there's a human story here. We've got 14 individuals that will receive layoff notices in the coming days. It's one of the hardest things that I have to do in this job.”

In a later interview, Mayor Anders Ibsen told The Urbanist that, for the last several months, he has been having discussions with lawmakers and leaders from other jurisdictions about new legislation that could allow jurisdictions to find new sources of revenue and break out of the restrictive revenue-sourcing cycle that repeatedly forces them into difficult budget cycles.

Ibsen said that the state may be facing severe budget challenges, but that isn’t just due to the economy. It’s also because of the state’s limited tax code. In many ways, he said, that sets local communities up to fail “because we have revenue sources that are always going to decline relative to inflation. That's why we're always in cut situations. That's not sustainable or fair, and it needs to change.”

“What you're going to see cities like Tacoma push for in the legislative session […] as the legislature approaches the tax code, is to make sure we don't have a two-tiered system where the state passes unfunded mandates down to us [which] gives us local taxing options,” Ibsen said. “We don't want to just continue having local taxing options. We want to have tools, but we also want to make sure that we have a unified tax code that is a shared burden for funding core services like public education, public safety, homelessness, you name it. It has to be a shared approach rather than robbing Peter to pay Paul.”
The city initially created the five-person HOPE Team three years ago, following the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests and the death of Manuel Ellis in Tacoma police custody in 2020.

In justifying cutting the team, the City appeared to suggest that the HOPE Team had been underutilized in its three years in existence. A slide from the council’s Oct. 27 meeting states that the HOPE Team answered about three calls per day in 2026, that it was hard to staff, and that the team was only available for limited hours. City policy also requires police officers or firefighters on the scene for safety reasons.
The Tacoma Fire Department also initially put out an Oct. 27 joint press release with the Tacoma Police Department explaining the pending cuts of the HOPE and CSO teams.

Though both departments pulled the press release shortly after its publication, the departments stated in that press release that both teams had “struggled to maintain intended staffing levels and have never been adequately positioned to effectively serve the community” from the get-go. The departments said that the teams responded to just a “fraction” of service calls the department received.

“One of the primary goals of HOPE was to relieve traditional first responders to focus their duty on calls where behavioral health issues were not the primary need for service,” the joint press release stated. “In many cases, HOPE and CSO efforts have proven redundant. Nearly all HOPE responses, for example, have also required the presence of paramedics, police officers, or firefighters. In reality, 99% of HOPE requests have required traditional first responder co-response since July 2023.”

But several members of the public argued that the HOPE Team — at barely three years old, with no studies showing its efficacy or lack thereof — was hardly getting a fair hearing, and that the City was cutting it prematurely.

“It’s accurate when everybody says that HOPE has been underfunded, understaffed, and underutilized, and I want to tell you that that is, in fact, your fault,” said Jonathan Pottle at the council’s Oct. 27 meeting. “Axing the HOPE Team is not an operational necessity. It’s an ideological choice, and it is a bad one.”

Both Theresa Power-Drutis, a longtime community organizer who works as the director of the New Connections re-entry program, and Barb Church, an environmental and community activist, told councilmembers that they needed to reconsider the way the HOPE Team is dispatched and accessible, rather than just eliminate it.

“If the team is eliminated, what happens? Police or fire will transport those in crisis to emergency rooms or shelters or jail. … However, shelters, jails, and emergency rooms do not provide resources for long-term mental health recovery,” added Calista Brown, another member of the public.

Like Power-Drutis and Church, Brown also suggested that the city “consider creative ways to enable HOPE’s operating at the capacity that truly meets community needs” and “how to offset ongoing understaffing, how to institute independent deployment.” She also highlighted that “police and fire have required co-response shutting down direct community access.”
“Review all the data that HOPE has collected so that the how and why of HOPE's effectiveness informs your decision to keep, eliminate, or truncate it,” Brown said.

“We have heard police officers say repeatedly that they are not trained to respond to mental health crises. […] A number of Tacoma police officers have described the HOPE Team as beneficial and stated they would like to see the HOPE Team expanded into late-night hours to be able to provide more extended support,” said Julie Andrzejewski, the co-chair of Indivisible Tacoma. “It's a cost-effective service. Eliminating it will result in greater costs, both human and financial.”

Gemini, a member of Tacoma Alliance Against Racist and Political Repression, seconded several other pro-HOPE commenters, and likewise underscored that the team didn’t even get a fighting chance. They also reminded the city of the financial cost of having no crisis responders.

“It’s kind of callous to talk about saving people's lives in the measure of dollars, but I understand we’re talking about a budget,” Gemini said. “I think we really need to think about how much money is spent when the police are dispatched to these crises. How much money was spent when SWAT was sent to Rhoda Butler’s house and shot her down and killed her? How much did that cost the city? How much did it cost the city to defend Manny Ellis’s murderers and pay out those murderers for the tunes of millions of dollars? […] We need to be weighing the real cost of police violence and [ … ] institutional violence against how much the HOPE Team costs, even if it was fully funded.”

During public comment at the council’s Nov. 10 meeting, Tacoma community member Nikki SnowKing member of the public who identified herself as Nikki reminded the council that it had made “an explicit promise to this community in the wake of Black Lives Matter and a call for accountability.”

“We were promised that Tacoma would fundamentally change its approach to public safety. You promised to invest in human-centered, non-police responses that protect rather than endanger our most vulnerable community members,” Nikki said. “The HOPE program is a direct realization of these promises. […] Dismantling the program is a clear retreat from the commitments that were made in Manuel Ellis’ name and to the Black and vulnerable communities of Tacoma.”

Ibsen told The Urbanist that “the promise that the city made was to keep Tacoma safe, while also partnering with the community to build on that trust, and the key behind that isn't the programs, it's the essence of what we're doing.”

articles.title: Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
articles.author:
<name>Patricia Smith, Professor of Economics Emeritus, University of Michigan</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/patricia-smith-336398"/>
paras: “Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people .

The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister.
“Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains.

I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story.
One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes.
My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults.

The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion .

Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price.
Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people.

That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.”

Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour , totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460 .
But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones.
Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours ), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits.
Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one.

AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities.

Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “ daughterhood penalty ,” or tax.

Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability.

Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives.
But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing.

Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores.
Patricia Smith is affiliated with the Ottawa County, MI Democratic Party.

articles.title: ‘SNL’ ‘Sister’ sketch nails the failures of US healthcare policy
articles.author:
<name>Jane Tavares, Senior Research Fellow and Lecturer of Gerontology, UMass Boston</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jane-tavares-1101291"/>
paras: A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “ Sister ” has gone viral. The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free?
The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families.

According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 63 million Americans provide ongoing care to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade. About 61% of these caregivers are women.

As researchers who study aging , long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers initially have better health and financial status than noncaregivers. But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts.
While societal gender expectations help explain why daughters often assume the bulk of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide.

One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance with everyday activities.

Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services. However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals or getting to the bathroom generally cannot rely on Medicare to pay for that assistance. Under Medicare’s home health benefit , limited personal care may be covered only when a patient also qualifies for skilled nursing or therapy services following surgery or a medical emergency and meets Medicare’s homebound requirements .

This distinction has enormous consequences. Someone over 65 may have comprehensive coverage for medical treatment but little help with the daily tasks necessary to remain safely at home. And this care is expensive: The national median cost of a home health aide was approximately US$6,688 per month, while residing in an assisted living facility averaged $6,141 per month in 2025.

For many older Americans, paying for the care they need is simply out of reach. A 2025 Harvard study found that 76% of households age 75 and older could not afford daily assistance from a home health aide after covering housing and basic living expenses. When paid care is unaffordable, those responsibilities frequently fall to relatives or, more rarely, close friends.
Medicaid , the public health insurance program for people who are low-income or have disabilities, is the country’s primary long-term care payer.

Unlike Medicare, Medicaid can pay for personal assistance at home, including help with bathing, dressing and other daily activities. The program covered nearly two-thirds of U.S. home care spending in 2023 . The divide between these programs dates back to 1965 , when Medicare was created to cover medical care for older adults, while Medicaid was designed to provide health coverage for people with low incomes. Over time, Medicaid became the country’s main payer for long-term care as the need for these costly services grew.
However, Medicaid eligibility generally requires meeting financial and other criteria that vary by state. Many older adults must exhaust most of their savings before qualifying for assistance.

Even being eligible for the program doesn’t guarantee that all needed services will be readily available. States have considerable discretion over the home-based services they provide, and many eligible people spend more than a year on waitlists to get services .

Having coverage, whether through Medicaid or the dwindling options available through private insurers to pay for long-term care, is only part of the challenge. Finding reliable help can be a struggle.

The nation’s direct care workforce, which includes home health aides and personal care assistants, faces persistent recruitment and retention challenges. These shortages may get worse as immigration enforcement and deportations reduce the workforce – one-third of these workers are foreign-born .
The median hourly wage for direct care work was $17.99 in 2025 , only $2-$3 per hour more than what fast-food workers earned.
When paid assistance is unavailable, insufficient or unaffordable, daughters and other relatives often fill the gaps by providing additional hours of care.

Family caregivers may have to work fewer hours or quit their jobs. These decisions not only reduce their income right away, but also whittle down their retirement savings and can depress the Social Security benefits they get in the future.

The federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave to care for certain family members, but the leave is unpaid. And caring for an older parent with chronic health conditions may continue for years after that leave runs out.
Because women are more likely to provide family care, they also face disproportionate exposure to these employment and financial risks.

Over the past two decades, some states have begun to address these gaps. California, New Jersey and about a dozen other states , for example, have launched paid family leave programs . In New York and some other states Medicaid is compensating family caregivers . Washington state is helping finance long-term care coverage .

In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris proposed expanding Medicare to cover more in-home assistance , an approach that would have addressed one of the main gaps in the current system. The Democratic presidential nominee’s proposal never moved beyond the campaign trail after Harris lost the 2024 election.

“Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch makes light of an uncomfortable family dynamic, but the issue extends well beyond whether brothers and sisters divide responsibilities fairly. Government policies are behind why so much of that responsibility falls on families in the first place.

When public programs do not cover the care older adults need, the need does not disappear. The work, and its financial and personal costs, simply shift to someone else. More often than not, that someone is a daughter.

articles.title: Trump administration may fund white South Africans to document ‘hateful rhetoric and violent acts’
articles.author:
<name>Susan Appe, Professor of Public Administration and Policy, University at Albany, State University of New York</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/susan-appe-347586"/>
paras: The U.S. State Department will reportedly give US$1 million to AfriForum , a nongovernmental organization that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners in South Africa.

The grant, first reported by ProPublica on Nov. 5, 2026 , would support research to document the “ hateful rhetoric and violent acts ” experienced by Afrikaners – descendants of white Dutch settlers who moved to South Africa in the 17th century.
As scholars who study foreign aid and civil society organizations , we would see U.S. support for AfriForum as a radical departure from the kinds of NGOs the U.S. has funded in the past .
The U.S. used foreign aid for decades to support efforts to build democracy abroad, enhance governance and strengthen human rights protections .

Until the second Trump administration, the primary government agencies distributing this assistance were the U.S. Agency for International Development, the State Department and the National Endowment for Democracy.

Past administrations called this assistance “ fundamental ” to the goals of U.S. foreign policy. By the end of President Joe Biden’s term, funding for democracy promotion had reached almost $3 billion annually .

Some of this money has supported NGOs engaged in civic participation and media independence. These efforts had been particularly important in fragile states and fledgling democracies, where civil society is especially at risk .
NGOs can also play an important role in reducing risks of violence between different ethnic and religious groups. By raising awareness about past atrocities, they can help stave off future violence .
The Trump administration suspended most U.S. foreign aid in January 2025 , soon after Donald Trump was sworn in as president for a second time.

It then dismantled USAID , the federal agency previously responsible for foreign aid and development assistance, and the White House compelled Congress to rescind billions of dollars of foreign aid spending . It has continued to take steps in that direction with or without lawmakers’ cooperation .
As a result, many lifesaving public health programs lost funding. This policy change has had an enormous human toll , which public health researchers have begun to quantify .

In addition, democracy assistance has been severely cut. USAID’s Democracy Fund , which funded programs dedicated to building democratic institutions and promoting fair elections and respect for human rights, was eliminated. The Department of State’s and National Endowment for Democracy’s funding and staffing for promoting democracy were also slashed .

In our research on NGOs that work on promoting democracy and the prevention of violence, we have seen and documented the benefits of these efforts . The organizations we have studied emphasize how people in South Africa and other countries with a history of identity-based violence can learn to live together across racial, ethnic and religious divides.
By contrast, AfriForum seeks to lift up Afrikaner identity and history , without any evident effort to bridge the divide between Afrikaners and other racial groups in South Africa.
It champions causes that have contributed to what South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, scholars and other analysts call a false narrative of a “ white genocide ” in that country.

In fact, researchers have found that Afrikaners and other white people in South Africa are less likely to be victims of crime and other forms of violence compared to other ethnic and racial groups in South Africa.
By funding AfriForum, the State Department would be elevating the dubious claims the group makes about the oppression of Afrikaners in South Africa.

And the Trump administration’s embrace of this false narrative goes beyond this grant for AfriForum. It explains why the U.S. has allowed thousands of white South Africans to come to the U.S. as refugees while denying admission to nearly all other refugees from the rest of the world.

articles.title: Is it genuine love – or obsessive passion? Kierkegaard, the father of existentialism, had some thoughts
articles.author:
<name>Ross Channing Reed, Assistant Teaching Professor of Philosophy, Missouri University of Science and Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/ross-channing-reed-2329706"/>
paras: Young love, honeymoon love, infatuation – these often feel spectacular. You have a burning need to be in constant contact, and you don’t want to let that person out of your sight.

It’s the start of many happy love stories. But at times, that feeling of obsession never fades – and the relationship never matures, or it even proves harmful. You know the relationship is bad for you, but you can’t end it. The more you try to break free, the more you feel stuck.

As a counselor , I often work with people whose relationships feel like an addiction, and who mistake that emotional roller coaster for love. And as a philosopher , I sometimes turn to 19th-century Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard to reflect on the differences between the two .

Kierkegaard is best known for his writing on religion. Today, he’s considered the father of existentialism , which stresses individual freedom, self-creation and personal responsibility. It is no surprise, then, that love is a central focus of his work. What he called “ethical” love expands freedom, while “aesthetic” love restricts it.

In 1843, a young Kierkegaard published “Either/Or,” his first book of philosophy – and one of his most important. The two volumes were published under the pseudonym “Victor Eremita,” one of many that Kierkegaard used throughout his life.

“Either/Or” makes a distinction between “ aesthetic ” and “ ethical ” ways of living. The aesthetic life is focused mainly on personal pleasure, while the ethical life expands to an awareness of how actions affect others.

Each way of life has its own form of love. Aesthetic love is one that you “fall” into. It comes over you. It is a powerful, seemingly irresistible force. The aesthetic lover “desires the individual absolutely,” Kierkegaard wrote .

Some lasting love begins that way, too. But aesthetic love lacks the trust and respect needed for stability. The yardstick of good and bad, right and wrong is centered on feelings and desires , not principles.
Feeling connected to and dependent on someone you don’t trust creates the tumult of addictive love. It can destroy the lover and the beloved, but often neither wants to give it up.

A counselee of mine fell instantly and madly in love. The passion was unlike anything he’d ever experienced. Though he doubted that the relationship could last, he told me he’d give up everything just to ride the wave for a year, or even six months. He was in the process of upending his life to be with her when the relationship failed a few months later. He went to a very dark place, doubting himself and the world.

This was a textbook example of Kierkegaard’s “aesthetic” love, which he talked about as an obsession or compulsion. In today’s terms, I’d consider it similar to addiction : a pattern that we feel compelled to continue , despite knowing how much it hurts us and others around us. Psychologists and philosophers debate how to define “addiction ,” and whether love can become one , but research indicates there can be similarities in behavior and brain activity between the two .

Obsessive, compulsive love often uses the relationship to escape the lover’s own issues. He or she may seem besotted with their beloved. In reality, though, they see the beloved as an object that can fill their emptiness or resolve their angst, rather than an independent human being with his or her own needs and desires.
At its root, Kierkegaard writes, aesthetic love is “ a kind of despair ,” rooted in estrangement from oneself , a kind of self-rejection or self-deception.
Obsessing over someone can serve to distract us from our self-rejection and emptiness. Aesthetic love seeks freedom through the other person, rather than freely loving them.

For Kierkegaard, there is an alternative: ethical love, rooted in virtue, choice and a solid sense of self. Kierkegaard discusses this kind of love in the second volume of “ Either/Or ” and in “ Works of Love ,” a book he published in 1847 under his own name.
Kierkegaard maintains that ethical love lacks the obsession and compulsion of aesthetic love. It is rooted in self-awareness, conscious choices and freedom, not thoughtless desire.

Ethical love is, in short, an ongoing conscious commitment, independent of the ebb and flow of emotion. This holds for all love, romantic or otherwise. Love is “a matter of conscience,” not impulse or calculation, Kierkegaard wrote in “Works of Love .”

It should be based on respect: treating other people as ends in and of themselves, not means to our own ends. In addition, ethical love is anchored in trust. Without these foundations, only the illusion of intimacy is possible.

Love centered on principles, not feelings, may sound like duty. But for Kierkegaard, it was freeing. No one should accept mistreatment: “Duty alone makes for genuine freedom. Spontaneous love makes a man free and in the next moment dependent,” he wrote .

This paradoxical view results from his idea that we must use our freedom to become ourselves , a concept he develops in his philosophy of existentialism. He maintains that human beings need an anchor in something greater than ourselves to fully utilize our freedom. Ultimately, for Kierkegaard, this was a personal God, but his insights can be illuminating even without reference to God.

Kierkegaard stresses that ethical love liberates not only the lover but the beloved: “The highest that one human being can do for another is to make him free, to help him stand alone.” This kind of love isn’t the joining of two into one – that is the enmeshment of obsessive, compulsive, addictive love. Ethical love is between two individual human beings who have chosen to trust, respect, support and forgive one another.

The distinction between the illusion of love and real love has a long history. Kierkegaard provides insight into how to effectively tell the difference – and how the power of real love lies in mutual liberation.

articles.title: El Niño created a skiers’ paradise in Chile – now it’s Sierra Nevada and Southern Rockies’ turn
articles.author:
<name>Steven R. Fassnacht, Professor of Snow Hydrology, Colorado State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/steven-r-fassnacht-1242332"/>
paras: El Niño has a reputation for being a skier’s dream, bringing lots of snow to California’s Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies. Tahoe-area resorts were already seeing the effects in mid-November 2026 as several feet of snow fell and some resorts prepared to open early for the season . But El Niño’s supercharged precipitation can spell trouble, too.

I’m an avid skier and snow scientist at Colorado State University. As the U.S. snow season begins amid what’s forecast to be one of the strongest El Niños on record , let’s take a look at what Chile’s very snowy winter might tell North America about what’s to come.
El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon that raises global temperatures and shifts weather patterns around the world.

It is defined by rising surface temperatures in the east-central tropical Pacific Ocean. When temperatures there are at least 0.5 degrees Celsius (0.9 Fahrenheit) warmer than average for three months, the world is in El Niño. The August-October average was 2.5 C warmer (36.5 F , making this among the warmest periods on record going back to 1950.

In the U.S., the southern half of the country tends to be wetter than usual during strong El Niños. That happens because the Pacific jet stream shifts southward, steering storms with it. The northern tier of the U.S. tends to be drier and warmer than normal.
That pattern is almost exactly what’s being forecast for the U.S. winter of 2026-27 . It’s also what the U.S. Southwest is already experiencing – to the extreme.

Powerful storms supercharged by El Niño in October and November caused widespread destructive flooding in the Four Corners region of New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado and Utah. Fast-melting snow and days of heavy rain flooded the San Juan River and Rio Grande, damaging hundreds of homes.
Community water systems and farms across the West need that precipitation after last winter delivered one of the lowest snow years on record for almost the entire western United States.

Major reservoirs in the Colorado River basin dropped during the year to their lowest levels since they were first filled . The two biggest – Lake Powell and Lake Mead – together supply water for about 40 million people and hydropower for hundreds of thousands of people.

The very low snowfall, as well as unusually warm midwinter temperatures that drove sublimation – the evaporation of snow – reduced water stored in the mountains. And that was followed by record-high summer temperatures .
Fall 2026’s heavy rain and snow may help make up for last year and start to alleviate a long-running drought that has been causing water supply problems across the western U.S. for a quarter century.

In a positive sign, Lake Powell rose with the recent rains. Overall, the Super El Niño conditions being forecast for 2026-27 are expected to bring more than average rain and snow this winter across much of the southern and central United States, where it’s also likely to alleviate drought.
Snow scientists like me keep an eye on the South American winter in El Niño years like this because it can give us a sense of what’s coming for North America.
Keep in mind that El Niño has been strengthening over the past few months – including through the South American winter that just ended.

South America saw a huge amount of snow , particularly in the central Chilean Andes. In some areas like Portillo , the snow accumulation was the deepest since the current drought began in 2010, and the deepest in the past 70 years north of Santiago at the top of the Limarí River.

The snow was a boon for Chile’s ski resorts . Valle Nevado got over 24 feet (7.3 meters) of snow and extended its ski season , originally scheduled to end in early October, into early December. Even the extremely dry Atacama Desert saw widespread snow followed by an explosion of spring flowers .

Historically, snowy winters in Chile have meant snowy winters for California’s Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies, too. The warm El Niño ocean allows the atmosphere to pick up more moisture in this zone than usual , and this brings snowstorms to the U.S. Southwest .

If that pattern holds this winter, the southern and central parts of the West should see well-above-average snowpack and active ski seasons, and those dangerously depleted reservoirs will have a chance to at least partially refill.

articles.title: History of automated train control
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: As I explained a few years ago , automating new lines and even existing lines would have many advantages. Even Sound Transit has recently considered automating the Ballard extension. Some people still consider automated train control (ATC) as unproven even though many airports (SeaTac, JFK AirTrain…) and subways use this technology such as Vancouver Skytrain and new lines on Hawaii and in Montreal already use the technology. Let’s look at the history .

Automating trains is much easier than having fully autonomous cars. As long as the trains run on tracks in a separate right of way, no complex video or even lidar systems are required but track sensors and a more powerful signaling and train control system. Platform doors are often added for additional safety.

Boston already started to experiment with automating trains in 1901. Berlin in 1928. Paris operated a short line from 1952 to 1957 but didn’t have funds for upgrades until the first main line was upgraded in 1966. More lines have been upgraded since. Tokyo started limited operation in 1962, more lines have been added since. Hitachi automated the Disney and Linimo monorail. London started tests in 1968. The Victoria Underground Line finally started fully automated operations in 1967.
While initially the trains still had a driver, fully driverless operation started in Kobe (Japan) and later in Lille (France), Barcelona and airports such as JFK.
In Nürnberg (Germany) they even allowed mixed operation between traditional and driverless trains in 2008.

More modern light metros such as Vancouver’s Skytrain (in 1985), London’s Dockland Light Railway (in 1987) and Copenhagen were designed as automated systems from the beginning allowing for shorter trains without a cab, smaller stations, and higher frequency. Recent new lines in Montreal (REM) and Hawaii also leveraged these advantages. Now many systems around the world are driverless. While Italian Ansaldo/Hitachi Rail STS developed their train systems around ATC, established rail provides ( Alstom Urbalis Fluence and Siemens Trainguard MT ) added ATC support to some of their existing rail offerings. Siemens AutomatedTrain effort is even automating regular heavy rail operation including the video detection of obstacles along the tracks.

As I explained in my prior post, Sound Transit had evaluated various modes in 2014. This included automated light metro systems such as Skytrain. At that time they decided on light rail technology for the spine to allow for both DSTT as well as at-grade operation. However, for some extensions Sound Transit is now planning, such as Ballard, it might be better to keep them separate rather than interlining them to leverage ATC advantages such as higher frequency and smaller stations.

As the northern Link line is fully grade separated, Link trains could even run fully automated from Everett to downtown. This would allow more precise acceleration and breaking, reduced headways (as close as 60sec) and faster turnaround at the end of the line, reducing the need for pocket tracks. Alstrom claims it reduces trackside equipment usage by up to 20% and energy consumption by up to 30%.
I hope Sound Transit would seriously consider automation where feasible.

articles.title: County Council Moves to Restore Weekend Vashon Water Taxi Service
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: An amendment approved this week by a King County Council budget committee is set to restore weekend fast ferry runs between Pier 50 in Downtown Seattle and Vashon Island after that service was sunsetted this fall. Via a half-penny increase to the county's Marine District property tax rate, seven round trips on Saturday and Sunday will be restored next year along with one additional Friday evening trip. In addition, the weekday mid-day trips currently on the schedule will be able to continue indefinitely.

The weekend runs had been enabled by a $1.1 million state earmark set aside in 2025 that ran out, an attempt by the legislature to supplement Washington State Ferries service. Prior to this spring when Sunday service got up-and-running, King County had not operated seven-day service on the Vashon water taxi since the 1990s. Without the water taxi in operation, anyone trying to get to Vashon Island has to utilize the state ferry terminals in West Seattle or Tacoma, which can add significant travel time for trips headed downtown.

Vashon Water taxi service has taken a big jump thanks to an expanded schedule. This September, the line provided 116% more rides than it did three years prior, with 30-40% of weekday riders now taking advantage of the added mid-day trips that hadn't previously existed. After seeing more than 155,000 riders in 2025, Vashon water taxi usage is on track to shatter that annual record, with more than 145,000 riders through the third quarter of 2026.

Put forward by Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda, this week's committee vote only received one vote in opposition, from South King County representative Steffanie Fain. Mosqueda, who represents the district that includes the fully unincorporated island, had been a champion for the water taxi at the legislature, working with State Senator Emily Alvarado (D-West Seattle, 34th Legislative District) on securing earmarks for the project in recent years.

"I want to thank the state legislature for the investments that they made in midday service and in weekend service. But we've heard very clearly from our state legislative partners, including the chair of the transportation committee in the Senate, that we should not expect there to be an ongoing source of revenue from the state legislature for water taxi service," Mosqueda told her colleagues.

Despite that clear shift away from providing funding for foot ferries at the legislature, many Vashon residents see King County fast ferry service as providing a critical fallback option when issues arise with Washington State Ferries service. Last month, when service on nearly every WSF route ground to a halt due to a crew shortage traced to a state employee labor dispute, the fast ferry was the only public option that Vashoners had to get on and off the island.

"Too many of our decision-makers see the water taxi as an optional nice-to-have service. But we all lived through the Oct. 5 ferry sick-out. The ferry shutdown made it plain that Vashon Island lives at the end of a fragile lifeline. We don’t have a bridge. We have the state ferries and the King County Metro water taxi," Amy Drayer, Rick Wallace and Wendy Aman, members of the Islanders for Ferry Action steering committee, wrote in the Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber last month. "Decision-makers need to know that we need more water transportation, not less."

King County is one of the few jurisdictions across the state allowed to operate a passenger ferry district, along with Kitsap Transit, thanks to a special carve-out in state law. The Mosquito Fleet Act, put forward by Rep. Greg Nance (D-23rd, Bainbridge), was intended to expand that pool by letting more cities, counties, and port districts in on the ability to use local funding tools, but it has run into headwinds at the legislature over the past two legislative sessions.

Marko Liias (D-Edmonds, 21st LD) has been the most outspoken skeptic of the Mosquito Fleet Act in the state Senate, but its chances may improve in the future. Liias, who has served in the legislature since 2008, recently announced a run for Snohomish County Executive.

"I do think it's important to make sure that our all of our county residents have have connectivity and and transit, especially so they can rely on systems that will not necessarily need a car," Councilmember Jorge Barón said. "And so I see this as part of the infrastructure, though it's not directly in my district, but I think my district residents will maybe use the water taxi to go on the weekends as well."

Earlier this year, King County secured a $22.1 million federal grant to expand the Downtown fast ferry terminal at Pier 50, with Metro's General Manager Michelle Allison noting that the agency will be able to double the capacity of the existing terminal with that funding. Space had been tight at the downtown terminal with expansion of Kitsap Transit's fast ferry service to Bremerton and Kingston, but those runs also relied on state funding that has now run out .

Councilmembers were persuaded to fund extra service to Vashon thanks in part to the ridership numbers that King County has been clocking. Under its Marine District authority, the county is able to levy a property tax of 7.5 cents on every $100,000 of taxable value, but currently only utilizes 0.8 cents. With Mosqueda's amendment, that will go up to 1.3 cents.

"This wasn't a high priority for me in terms of this particular budget, but I did ask your office for the ridership numbers, [and] I heard from one of your constituents by email asking that this service be continued, and so I did a little bit more digging into it and what it would cost, and it is remarkably affordable," Council Budget Chair Rod Dembowski said to Mosqueda during this week's meeting. "I don't think lives stop midday, and they don't stop on the weekend."
The Marine District tax increase is set to be included in the county's mid-biennial budget update, set to be voted on November 24.

articles.title: County Council Advances RapidRide R Plan to Consolidate Route 7 Stops
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Plans to bring RapidRide to the Rainier Valley took a step forward Tuesday with a King County committee vote to approve the planned alignment and stop locations for the future R Line between Rainier Beach and Downtown Seattle. A major priority for King County Executive Girmay Zahilay, the overhaul of the existing Route 7 has drawn concerns around transit access, with a number of existing bus stops used by riders set to be consolidated together when the RapidRide line is built.

Slated to open by 2032, the $91.2 million RapidRide line along Rainier Avenue is set to come with infrastructure upgrades at stops, along with some speed and reliability upgrades on top of bus lanes that have already been added by the City of Seattle in recent years.

The 7 is already one of the most frequent buses in the system, which contributes to it being the second-busiest route Metro runs. As such, significant improvements in bus frequency aren't likely, but more trips may be added on nights and weekends.

Zahilay's administration is eyeing ways to accelerate rollout of the R Line, proposing a 2027 budget that would advance nearly two-thirds of the funding for the project in the hopes of showing a firmer commitment to the Seattle Department of Transportation, which is planning related upgrades along Rainier in future years.

While stop consolidation has traditionally been part of the RapidRide package elsewhere, Metro's plans to eliminate high-use stops like S Cloverdale Street and S Charles Street have proven unpopular among existing 7 riders. In addition, the R Line would modify the 7's route to directly serve Rainier Beach Station, eliminating service south of S Henderson Street including on the S Prentice Street loop where some 7 trips currently terminate.

The R Line has been on the books for over a decade, envisioned as one of a slate of transit corridors to be funded by the 2015 Seattle Transportation Levy. But the project was put on hold in 2021 in the wake of pandemic-related budget cuts.

When Metro restarted outreach on the project earlier this summer, the plans for stop consolidation – controversial even at the time – were largely the same, though a pair of stops around Mount Baker did get re-added ahead of transmittal to the County Council in response to feedback this fall .

King County Metro has downplayed the impact of that planned stop consolidation, noting that 12 out of 16 stops north of Henderson Street set to be eliminated are currently served by other buses – even if those buses go in very different directions, like the crosstown Route 50. However, the ordinance adopted Tuesday does not actually set future stop locations for the R Line in stone, instead requiring the county council to be notified if there are any changes to the plan.

Councilmember Rhonda Lewis, who was Zahilay's top aide before winning appointment to the District 2 seat that he represented until being elected County Executive last year, praised the R Line in comments ahead of Tuesday's vote, while at the same time noting the potential impacts that could come from having fewer bus stops on Rainier.

"For older riders and riders with disabilities, the walk to the next stop is no small thing. Many neighbors have also told me that they feel safer waiting at Cloverdale than at the stops nearby," Lewis said. "Today's vote settles the route and its stations. However, I'm grateful to hear that Metro has committed to keep the conversation with constituents going through design and construction to ensure community concerns are heard. My constituents in District 2 have waited a long time for this line, and I am proud to see it move forward today."
Lewis's colleague Claudia Balducci struck a much more concerned tone.

"When we hear from members of the surrounding community as plaintively as we have heard from this community that this service will actually be a degradation because of loss of stops," Balducci said. "Frequent and reliable service is only as good as people's ability to get on it, and I'm very concerned that I'm hearing, this kicking of the can down the road: 'Yes, we'll keep talking to the community.' But we are today, and at the council meeting [next week], we'll be taking a vote to reduce access to transit in this corridor."

Committee chair Steffanie Fain afforded Zahilay's administration and King County Metro more deference than Balducci. Fain represents South King County, where Metro is currently building the RapidRide I line – a project that has had its own twists and turns when it comes to getting to construction.

"I did appreciate that Metro added back two stops based on that feedback, and so I think that the RapidRide R line won't work without community partnerships, and that they are building those and are responding to those," Fain said. "And I think the community appreciates that. If I could be so bold as to say that I know that this is ongoing work and, nothing's perfect, but certainly I appreciate the collaboration with the community."

Balducci also raised issues with accelerating the funding for the R Line without a clear picture of what exactly that funding will achieve in 2027, while the project is still in planning. Metro is currently facing an uncertain financial future, with the agency's fiscal reserves set to start to run out by the early 2030s, but decisions around how to deal with that reality aren't expected to be put forward until next year's budget cycle.

"We are holding that money unspent intentionally in 2027, apparently because our friends at SDOT need to see that there's money sitting in a box in order to feel comfortable moving forward," Balducci said. "That is not a resounding statement of support for this project by our colleagues in SDOT. And also, what a waste to put aside tens of millions of dollars for no purpose."

Transit advocates are still waiting to see a full analysis of the time savings that will come from the full R Line package, which as presented earlier this year will leave out transit priority treatments along one of the 7's most problematic stretches – along S Jackson Street through the International District.

"That's what I'd love to see because I think then we could have a better conversation about okay, maybe there's places where it really makes sense to eliminate stops, but if you're just making people's walks longer and you're not actually making the commute time significantly shorter or the travel time..." Anna Zivarts, founder of the Nondrivers Alliance, told The Urbanist last month on a bus tour of Rainier Avenue.

Zivarts has been pushing to broaden the conversation about what the R Line can do to improve transit access, potentially even looking at different transit corridors that aren't available today, including all-day connections directly to Capitol Hill and First Hill.

"There's a lot of folks using the bus to travel locally within Rainier Valley, and commuting to downtown as efficiently as possible is not necessarily the top priority for a lot of folks who are using transit right now on this road," Zivarts said. "So we need to make sure we're meeting those needs with whatever investment [we make]. We'd love more investments in transit, yes, but let's make sure we're serving the people who are relying on it currently in this area."

Lewis did not participate in Tuesday's committee vote, which was unanimous. In fact, the county's transportation committee includes no members who represent Seattle, in what is likely a first in King County history. Next week, former state Senator Rebecca Saldaña will take office as Zahilay's permanent replacement to represent District 2, likely just a few hours after this ordinance gets a full council vote.
Though the R Line is moving forward, the conversation around its exact design is certain to continue.

articles.title: Alternative Transit Modes
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: As I explained in an earlier guideway post, Sound Transit chose light rail technology to make it easier to use the existing transit tunnel and to run and stop at grade but many new technologies have been developed since. As Sound Transit builds a lot more elevated and tunneled sections and opens new lines in urban areas, it may need to reevaluate that decision. Sound Transit and Metro already use buses, heavy rail (for Sounder), ferries, and trams. Other cities like San Francisco, Mexico, and Paris use even more different modes like people movers and gondolas. In that post I talked about monorail and maglev guiderail systems. They are easier and faster to build due to prefabricated guideways, are slicker and therefore visually less obtrusive, and may offer easier maintenance.

As Sound Transit is facing escalating construction costs and feels it cannot accommodate traditional elevated trains downtown, it may be a good time to evaluate these and other alternative transit modes. Monorail systems have opened in Bangkok, and TSB has built a maglev test line in China and is looking at several options in Germany. Swyft Cities (working with Whoosh Solutions) and Ottobahn are working on cabins which hang from a guideway like the Wuppertaler Schwebebahn and provide personal rapid transit (PRT).

Similar to a Waymo or Zoox robotaxi, Swyft Cities and Ottobahn offer more route flexibility, are called via phone app, and have small individual cabins with an electric motor. Unlike a robotaxi, they use airspace and don’t get stuck in traffic, they are confined to its track network, have specific parking/staging areas, use electric motors with track power, and use small stations. While Swyft cabins travel on fixed cables (similar to a gondola or the RopeTaxi but those are propelled by the cable), Ottobahn cabins travel on regular tracks at 37mph. For longer distances Ottobahn claims up to 150mph. Both use track switches to guide cabins to their destination.

Ottobahn cabins hang off a bogie which is powered by an electric motor with regular wheels and steel tracks. Cabins either stop at elevated stations or can employ a lift mechanism which drops the cabin to the sidewalk for on- and off-boarding. Ottobahn claims they can support 6000 riders per hour in each direction, or even more with a favorable network design. Similar to a monorail, their track is supported by towers about 120ft apart and between 15 and 30ft high. The track can also cross longer distances over rivers and other obstacles akin to a suspension bridge. Cabins can usually climb up to 7%, with extra support even 12%. That may allow a ship canal crossing.
Swyft is hoping to start projects in Queenstown, Miami, or Los Angeles. Ottobahn started construction of its first network in Phuket .

Traditional train lines serve stations along a linear corridor. Turning a train around at the end of the line takes time as the operator usually has to switch from one end of the train to the other. Lines may branch towards the outer area of a network, but that splits the headway on each branch. As automated train systems do not need to worry about a driver, they can switch direction more easily and offer a bit more flexibility. For example, they can serve short stub lines by backing in and out, though that may impact travel time. PRT systems are not bound to any fixed line/schedule, can use a more elaborate track network, branch on demand, skip stations, and only stop as necessary. Though each cabin may be smaller, short headways may still allow for sufficient capacity.

Any of these systems promise simpler/faster guideway and station construction, easier integration into the existing urban infrastructure, more flexible branching capabilities, and more convenience for riders. It may be worthwhile to consider them for West Seattle or Ballard and other future lines.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.
